49566.etyen:
The lowercase form of S. Its modern rounded shape developed from cursive and minuscule forms of Latin S. In medieval and early modern writing, round ⟨s⟩ coexisted with long ⟨ſ⟩; long ⟨ſ⟩ was generally used initially and medially, while round ⟨s⟩ was normally used word-finally. The round form eventually became standard in all positions as long ⟨ſ⟩ fell out of general use around the beginning of the 19th century.
The Latin letter was adopted through Etruscan 𐌔 (s) from a western form of Ancient Greek Σ (S, “sigma”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤔 (š, “šīn; tooth”). The Norwegian letter name ess ul / The uppercase form of s. From Latin S, through Etruscan 𐌔 (s), from a western form of Ancient Greek Σ (S, “sigma”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤔 (š, “šīn; tooth”). The shape and alphabetic position of Greek sigma continue Phoenician šīn, whose sibilant sound was adapted to Greek /s/. The Greek name σίγμα (sígma, “sigma”) may have been influenced by Phoenician 𐤎 (s, “sāmek”), while the latter letter otherwise developed into Greek Ξ (X, “xi”). 118942.etyen:
From edel + kastanje, literally “noble chestnut”, with edel in its sense “high-quality, superior”. The first element is from Middle Low German ēdel (“noble”), and is related to adel; for the deeper history of the second element, see kastanje. Synchronically, the modifier distinguishes the true, edible chestnut from the unrelated hestekastanje.
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk edelkastanje, Danish ædelkastanje and German Edelkastanie.

1000094.etyen:
Internationalism, based ultimately on Arabic سُودَان (sūdān, “black people”), a plural of أَسْوَد (ʔaswad, “black”), through the historical expression بِلَاد السُّودَان (“land of the Black people”). The expression was used by medieval Arabic geographers for the region south of the Sahara, and the modern country takes its name from this older regional designation.
Parallel international forms include Norwegian Nynorsk Sudan, Danish Sudan, Swedish Sudan, German Sudan and English Sudan.

1000606.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately based on Middle French Madagascar, from the medieval form Madageiscar, recorded by Marco Polo. The deeper origin of the medieval name is unknown.
A traditional hypothesis connects Madageiscar with Arabic مَقْدِيشُو (maqdīšū, “Mogadishu”), the name of the Somali city, through a geographical confusion in Marco Polo's account. Another proposal connects the name with Arabic جَزِيرَة المَالَائِيّ (jazīra(t) al-mālāʔiyy, “Island of Mālāī”), a name occurring in the geographical tradition of al-Idrisi. Neither explanation is certain.

en.g: a female given name from Norwegian

1004702.etyen:
Short form of Otilie, one of several Norwegian spellings of a female given name going back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda. The Old High German names are formed from the Germanic name element reflected in *audaz (“wealth, riches”), with a pet-name or diminutive ending. The final -a gives the name a form similar to other Norwegian female given names ending in -a.
Compare Danish Tilja, Swedish Tilja and English Tilly (“female given name”).
